Week 90 Appendix: The Week the Clock Held Still

Amid fund diversions, an ICE shooting, and claims of unlimited power, courts and citizens pushed back hard enough to hold the line.

This was a week of accelerating institutional strain as the midterm campaign intensified alongside open assertions of unchecked executive authority. Trump explicitly claimed "I can do whatever I want," diverted DHS funds for self-promotional ads, floated nationalizing election seizure with a convicted election denier, and suggested letting Iran destroy Los Angeles and San Diego — rhetoric met with bipartisan alarm. ICE's shooting of a man with a child present in Manhattan, mass ICE detentions of U.S. citizens, and DHS's covert targeting of voter-registration groups revealed an enforcement apparatus turning inward against civil society ahead of the election. Simultaneously, courts and plaintiffs pushed back: a federal judge voided DOJ's voter-roll collection scheme, the DNC and Common Cause sued over taxpayer-funded political ads, and a defendants' union formed to counter NSPM-7 prosecutions. Financial entanglements (Qatar jet, crypto profits, pardoned-donor business deals) and retiring senators' candid warnings about authoritarian drift rounded out a week defined by brazen self-dealing paired with resilient, if strained, institutional resistance.

Power and Authority

  1. Trump ordered Office of Management and Budget to divert $20 million in Department of Homeland Security funds for television ads praising himself: Redirecting congressionally appropriated DHS funds for campaign-style self-promotion bypasses legislative control over spending and raises emoluments concerns. (2026-10-03)
  2. Trump announced distribution of Medicare Part B premium payments to seniors from the Medicare Improvement Fund, tying future larger payments to a Republican midterm win: Using a health program fund for pre-election cash payments and linking a bigger payout to an election outcome blurs the line between governance and campaign inducement. (2026-10-04)
  3. Trump promised $5,000 payments to all adult citizens if Republicans win the midterm elections: A presidential pledge of direct cash payments contingent on an election outcome uses the power of the office to influence voters without a specified funding mechanism. (2026-10-06)
  4. Trump signed an executive order deferring diesel fuel excise taxes and penalties through December 31, 2026: Unilaterally suspending federal tax collection and directing exploration of permanent forgiveness extends executive reach into tax and appropriations authority reserved to Congress. (2026-10-05)
  5. Jared Kushner negotiated with Russian President Putin to purchase sanctioned Lukoil assets at depressed prices, benefiting Trump-linked investors: Using informal White House-linked channels to arrange a lucrative deal with a wartime adversary raises conflict-of-interest and foreign-influence concerns over U.S. foreign policy. (2026-10-03)
  6. U.S. Southern Command conducted its 70th strike on a Caribbean boat, killing four more people without public evidence or judicial process: Continuing extrajudicial lethal strikes without transparent legal justification bypasses courts and due process in matters normally handled by the justice system. (2026-10-04)
  7. Trump stated he could have prosecuted Clinton, Biden, and Obama but chose restraint, then asserted "I can do whatever I want": A sitting president's explicit claim of unlimited personal power undermines constitutional limits and signals willingness to use prosecution selectively against rivals. (2026-10-07)
  8. Trump suggested at campaign rallies that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego, calling the loss "a small price to pay": A president publicly accepting the destruction of major American cities by a foreign adversary undermines the basic duty to protect citizens and alarmed officials across party lines. (2026-10-05)
  9. Trump met with election denier Tina Peters at the White House to discuss seizing voting machines and ballots nationwide: Presidential engagement with a convicted election official over plans to seize ballots threatens the constitutional process for certifying elections and the peaceful transfer of power. (2026-10-05) [single source]
  10. Trump endorsed building a Camp David-style presidential retreat on his own golf club property: Linking federal presidential facilities to a privately owned Trump property blurs the separation between public office and personal financial interest. (2026-10-09)
  11. Trump announced a deal with Putin for Russia to supply growing volumes of diesel fuel to the U.S. market ahead of the midterms: Striking an energy deal with a wartime adversary just before elections drew accusations of funding Russia's war effort and using foreign policy for domestic political gain. (2026-10-09)

Institutions and Governance

  1. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended executions through year-end and ordered an independent inquiry after the state's prison chief failed to implement reforms following botched executions: Executive suspension of executions and an independent probe respond to documented institutional failure to follow safety recommendations in capital punishment procedures. (2026-10-03)
  2. Justice Samuel Alito gave a rare interview discussing his annual contemplation of retirement and the personal toll of the Dobbs decision: A sitting justice's public remarks on possible retirement and the Court's strained independence affect public understanding of the Court's stability and future composition. (2026-10-04) [single source]
  3. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the government an administrative stay pending appeal in Rogoff v. Trump without ruling on the merits: A procedural stay keeps a legal challenge to an administration action in limbo, illustrating the ongoing churn of litigation testing executive conduct. (2026-10-04)
  4. Senate approved bipartisan legislation easing mental health treatment barriers for pilots and air traffic controllers: Removing stigma-driven regulatory barriers to treatment-seeking among aviation professionals strengthens both worker rights and public safety through better oversight design. (2026-10-05) [single source]
  5. Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County on whether federal law preempts state climate-damage lawsuits: A ruling favoring oil companies could eliminate state-level climate accountability litigation nationwide, reshaping the balance between federal preemption and state authority. (2026-10-05)
  6. District Court (N.D. Cal.) allowed two plaintiffs to voluntarily dismiss claims without prejudice in Global Nurse Force v. Trump: A routine partial dismissal narrows one ongoing legal challenge to an administration policy while leaving other plaintiffs' claims intact. (2026-10-05)
  7. Senate Democrats signaled they will not confirm Trump Supreme Court nominees if they win control of the chamber: A pledge to block judicial confirmations regardless of nominee qualifications signals deepening politicization of the confirmation process across both parties. (2026-10-05)
  8. Supreme Court issued a batch of October 5 orders denying stays, granting certiorari with vacatur and remand in multiple cases, and permitting Solicitor General participation in two arguments: Routine orders deciding procedural questions in immigration, criminal, and election cases shape which disputes receive further judicial review this term. (2026-10-05)
  9. Federal judge Paul Engelmayer ordered the Pentagon and DOJ to produce the legal memo justifying boat strikes and disclose who reviewed it: Judicial demand for disclosure of a classified legal opinion underlying lethal military action reasserts court oversight of executive claims of authority. (2026-10-06)
  10. Samuel Alito stated he does not anticipate the Court overturning Obergefell v. Hodges: A justice's public prediction about the fate of a major constitutional precedent shapes public expectations about the Court's direction on established rights. (2026-10-06)
  11. District Court (D.D.C.) denied both a preliminary injunction and a motion to dismiss in Smith v. U.S. Department of Defense over a Pentagon ombudsman's retaliation claim: The court left open unresolved First Amendment questions about retaliation against a public employee for critical speech made within her official role. (2026-10-06)
  12. Congress enacted the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025 and the Improving Social Security's Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act into law: Bipartisan enactment of oversight and consumer-protection legislation reflects functioning legislative process affecting federal spending scrutiny and identity-theft victim services. (2026-10-07)
  13. Common Cause filed suit challenging a $20 million DHS-funded advertising contract featuring Trump as an illegal use of appropriated funds for campaign purposes: The lawsuit tests whether executive branch use of appropriated funds for self-promotional ads violates statutory limits on propaganda spending and equal-protection principles. (2026-10-07)
  14. District Court (D.D.C.) granted in part a stay of DHS's biometrics policy for detained immigration applicants in Z. v. DHS, finding the policy likely arbitrary and capricious: The ruling found DHS failed to justify a policy that risked preventing detained applicants from pursuing their immigration cases, reinstating stronger procedural protections. (2026-10-07)
  15. Supreme Court denied habeas corpus, mandamus, and certiorari petitions in the capital case of Jamaal Howard, with Justice Jackson dissenting from one denial: Final denials of emergency review in a death penalty case close off further judicial avenues before the scheduled execution, with one justice registering dissent. (2026-10-07)
  16. Democracy Docket analysis reported that the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais decision gutted Voting Rights Act protections, prompting a wave of Southern redistricting: Removal of a foundational federal voting-rights constraint enabled Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, and Tennessee legislatures to redraw maps targeting Black voting power. (2026-10-08)
  17. Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration to stop use of taxpayer funds for self-promotional campaign ads: The lawsuit raises constitutional separation-of-powers and appropriations questions about executive use of public money for partisan self-promotion during the midterm season. (2026-10-08)
  18. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan ruled that DOJ's collection of unredacted state voter rolls for cross-checking against immigration databases was unlawful: The ruling blocks a federal attempt to seize control of voter-roll data from states, protecting citizens from erroneous removal from registration lists ahead of the midterms. (2026-10-08)
  19. Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered Tennessee to preserve all evidence from the execution chamber after Christa Pike survived lethal injection: Judicial intervention to preserve evidence from a failed execution addresses concerns about concealment and supports future legal challenges over cruel and unusual punishment. (2026-10-08)
  20. Department of Justice filed a complaint against Denver challenging its mask ban and identification requirements for federal law enforcement officers: The suit tests whether a city can require federal officers to display identification and forgo masks during enforcement operations within its jurisdiction. (2026-10-08)
  21. Department of Justice filed motions defending a rule rescinding the regulatory definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act: Defending a narrowed definition of species harm in court affects the scope of federal environmental protections against habitat destruction. (2026-10-08)
  22. New Mexico Wildlife Federation and border-region groups sued the Department of the Interior and Department of Defense over the transfer of 110,000 acres to military control for border security: The suit challenges executive authority to transfer public lands and militarize immigration enforcement without statutory authorization, raising separation-of-powers questions. (2026-10-08)
  23. Supreme Court issued an emergency stay of a Fourth Circuit judgment in FCC v. Sherrod Brown: An emergency Supreme Court stay involving a federal agency and a sitting senator signals a significant unresolved dispute requiring expedited high-court attention. (2026-10-08)
  24. Manhattan District Attorney's Office opposed Luigi Mangione's motion to dismiss state murder charges on double jeopardy grounds: The filing tests the boundary between federal and state prosecution authority and New York's double jeopardy protections in a high-profile case. (2026-10-09)
  25. Supreme Court earlier in 2026 upheld state laws excluding transgender girls and women from female sports: The ruling narrowed transgender rights and gave legal cover for Republican campaign messaging attacking Democratic candidates during the midterm cycle. (2026-10-09)
  26. Disney and ABC filed a federal court challenge to the FCC's early review of broadcast licenses for eight ABC-owned stations: The challenge argues the license review retaliates against disfavored editorial decisions, testing whether regulatory power can be used to coerce broadcast content. (2026-10-09)
  27. Arlington County Board filed suit against the Trump administration to block construction of a presidential triumphal arch in Washington, D.C.: A local government's legal challenge to a federal monument project tests the limits of executive discretion over public space and spending priorities. (2026-10-09)
  28. Democratic congressional leadership outlined plans to pursue subpoena-backed investigations into Trump family business dealings, Epstein files, Pentagon contracts, and other matters if they win control of Congress: Articulated oversight plans show how a change in congressional control could restore subpoena power and committee capacity for checking executive conduct. (2026-10-09)

Economic Structure

  1. Federal Register publication formalized Executive Order 14435 deferring diesel fuel excise taxes through December 31, 2026: Official publication of the tax-deferral order confirms an executive attempt to suspend federal revenue collection and explore permanent tax forgiveness without legislative approval. (2026-10-09)
  2. AM General employees and PAC donated tens of thousands of dollars to key appropriations committee members after Congress funded armored vehicles the Army said it did not need: A pattern of defense-contractor donations following congressional funding of unneeded equipment raises concerns about pay-to-play influence on military appropriations. (2026-10-05)
  3. Iowa state government approved a $1.36 billion incentive package for a new steel plant costing at least $777,000 per job created: An incentive package far exceeding typical per-job costs, tied to a politically promoted deal, raises questions about misuse of public resources for electoral messaging. (2026-10-05)
  4. Gulf oil producers and shipping companies increased oil shipments from the Persian Gulf despite wartime attack risks, driving freight costs to $40 million per trip: War-driven disruption and record shipping costs in a critical energy corridor illustrate the economic toll of ongoing military conflict on global markets. (2026-10-05)
  5. Washington, D.C. tourism industry experienced steep declines as international visitors cited anger over Trump's tariffs, immigration policy, and treatment of allies: A sharp drop in international tourism to the capital reflects reputational damage to U.S. soft power resulting from administration policies and rhetoric. (2026-10-05) [single source]
  6. Trump administration announced sweeping tariffs on trading partners, then repeatedly reversed, modified, and exempted them, creating sustained trade-policy uncertainty: Volatile tariff policy discourages business investment and planning, generating macroeconomic uncertainty that affects employment and growth nationwide. (2026-10-05) [single source]
  7. FDA issued routine medical device classifications, drug withdrawal corrections, and regulatory determinations affecting pharmaceutical and device markets: Ordinary regulatory actions on device classification and drug approvals shape market access and safety oversight for patients and manufacturers. (2026-10-06)
  8. Trump accepted a $400 million aircraft gift from Qatar for use as Air Force One: Accepting a massive foreign gift as a sitting president raises constitutional emoluments concerns and questions about foreign influence over the executive branch. (2026-10-06)
  9. Trump disclosed $2.2 billion in business earnings during his first year back in office, including $1.4 billion from a family cryptocurrency venture: The scale of presidential business income while in office raises constitutional emoluments concerns and questions about personal enrichment from the presidency. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  10. Trump accepted a memecoin dinner invitation for top crypto investors while personally profiting roughly $636 million from the coin last year: A pay-to-access dinner tied to a presidential cryptocurrency venture illustrates ongoing monetization of the office during an election cycle. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  11. Federal Transit Authority announced plans to steer infrastructure grants toward areas with higher birthrates and marriage rates: Conditioning federal infrastructure funding on demographic reproductive metrics reflects a racialized ideology and departs from neutral public-goods allocation criteria. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  12. Food & Water Watch reported U.S. household water prices rose 62% over the past decade, outpacing inflation and wages: Rapidly rising water costs strain household budgets and disproportionately burden low-income families heading into the midterm elections. (2026-10-06)
  13. Trump meme coin firm insiders offered perks to encourage public buying of cryptocurrency while moving $70 million of insider holdings toward sale: Insiders selling while promoting purchases to the public raises concerns about market manipulation connected to the president's name and image. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  14. Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital announced multi-billion-dollar loan commitments and contracts to private semiconductor, quantum, and missile-defense firms: Large military-linked loans and contracts to private technology and defense firms illustrate deepening public-private entanglement in strategic industrial policy. (2026-10-07)
  15. EPA approved multiple state air-quality implementation plans affecting ozone, nitrogen oxide, and sulfur dioxide standards across several states: Routine approvals of state environmental regulations shape enforceable federal air-quality standards affecting industrial emissions and public health protections. (2026-10-08)
  16. Department of Transportation pursued regulatory changes weakening airline passenger protections on pricing disclosure and flight-disruption compensation: Rolling back consumer protections without new evidence of harm favors airline industry interests over passenger rights and government's protective role. (2026-10-08) [single source]
  17. FDA extended its safety review of mifepristone into 2027 following pressure from anti-abortion groups: A politically pressured, prolonged regulatory review of an approved medication risks weaponizing the FDA process to restrict reproductive-health access. (2026-10-08)
  18. DHS purchased five aircraft at a considerable markup from a political donor of outgoing Secretary Kristi Noem, including a $108 million luxury jet: A high-value procurement from a political donor at inflated prices on an outgoing official's last day raises concerns about corruption in government contracting. (2026-10-09)

Civil Rights and Dissent

  1. Tom Morello and participating musicians organized the Power to the People festival with voter-registration resources and proceeds donated to a nonpartisan voting-access group: A large-scale concert combining political speech with voter-registration drives exercised First Amendment rights and promoted civic participation ahead of the midterms. (2026-10-03)
  2. Dário Sánchez and Texas state prosecutors faced repeatedly amended terrorism-related charges for moderating an online chat tied to a protest he did not attend: Prosecuting a non-attendee over online chat moderation, alongside extreme sentences for co-defendants, shows weaponized use of the justice system against political association. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  3. NSPM-7 Defendants Union launched a collective defense organization offering legal clinics and coordinated strategy for people prosecuted under the president's NSPM-7 memorandum: Formation of a defendants' union represents organized civil-society resistance to government prosecution of protest activity across multiple movements. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  4. Governor Gavin Newsom publicly denounced Trump's suggestion that Iran attack Los Angeles and San Diego as "deranged and dangerous": A state executive's public rejection of presidential rhetoric endorsing attacks on American cities marks a significant institutional pushback on public-safety grounds. (2026-10-06)
  5. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria rejected Trump's framing of San Diego as an acceptable loss, stating the city is not expendable: A local executive's rejection of being characterized as a disposable casualty in geopolitical rhetoric asserts municipal duty to protect residents. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  6. Voto Latino Foundation and Hispanic Federation launched a six-figure voter mobilization effort targeting underrepresented Latino voters in Texas's Rio Grande Valley: Grassroots voter-mobilization campaigns aim to expand electoral participation among historically underrepresented eligible voters in a swing region. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  7. FBI arrested an 18-year-old after supplying him with an AK-47 in an undercover sting targeting the Mall of America: A nearly two-year undercover operation culminating in federal agents providing a weapon to a suspect raises serious entrapment and civil-liberties concerns. (2026-10-07) [single source]
  8. NAACP sued the Trump administration challenging plans to deploy roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to midterm polling sites: The suit argues the planned deployment lacks statutory authority and risks voter intimidation, raising constitutional concerns about federal interference in elections. (2026-10-07) [single source]
  9. Bo French tweeted outrage at Indian American children attending a University of Texas football game, sparking broader anti-Indian sentiment online: A state candidate's public targeting of an ethnic minority group normalized exclusionary rhetoric against an immigrant community in political discourse. (2026-10-07)
  10. DOJ sought a federal criminal indictment of former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson for alleged perjury in her January 6 congressional testimony: Prosecuting a key January 6 witness through an unusual DOJ channel raises concerns about retaliation against testimony damaging to the former administration. (2026-10-08)
  11. Pentagon Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a public, livestreamed military execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, the first in over 60 years: Plans to broadcast a military execution represent a significant departure from past practice, drawing bipartisan criticism over dignity and spectacle in capital punishment. (2026-10-08)
  12. Texas Department of Criminal Justice executed Jamaal Howard by pentobarbital hours after the same drug caused complications in another execution: Proceeding with an execution using a drug shown to fail hours earlier raises acute concerns about courts failing to prevent foreseeable cruel and unusual punishment. (2026-10-08)
  13. Homeland Security Investigations investigated over 150 voter-registration organizations and considered undercover operations against them, finding no derogatory information in most cases: Broad federal investigation of civic organizations, including civil rights groups, under the guise of election security risks chilling protected political activity. (2026-10-08)
  14. ICE collected tens of millions of voter records for integration into a deportation-targeting database: Mass collection of voter data by immigration enforcement for deportation targeting threatens legal residents and chills participation in the democratic process. (2026-10-08)
  15. Billionaire donors funded California Proposition 39, a ballot measure requiring voter identification at polls and on mail ballots: Large donor funding behind a voter-ID ballot measure could restrict ballot access for eligible voters lacking required documentation, narrowing participation. (2026-10-08)
  16. ICE agent Brenden Cuni shot a man in the neck during an enforcement operation in Manhattan's Marble Hill with a 5-year-old child present in the vehicle: An immigration enforcement shooting with a child in the vehicle, involving an agent with a documented history of unlawful arrests, raises serious use-of-force accountability concerns. (2026-10-08)
  17. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded ICE's removal from the city after the shooting, criticizing agents' tactics as terrorizing residents: A mayor's public demand for federal agency withdrawal highlights escalating tension between local government and immigration enforcement over public safety. (2026-10-08)
  18. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended ICE's shooting tactics and dismissed the mayor's criticism as dangerous: A federal official's defense of controversial enforcement tactics amid public outcry reflects reluctance to hold immigration enforcement accountable for use of force. (2026-10-09)
  19. ProPublica reporting found ICE detained U.S. citizens over 500 times during the second Trump administration, including at least 70 children and teens: Mass detention of citizens, including children, by immigration authorities without clear legal basis undermines constitutional due-process protections. (2026-10-09) [single source]
  20. Trump administration transferred undocumented children living with their parents into ORR custody while detaining the parents: Reclassifying children to separate them from detained parents already residing in the country revives family-separation practices with constitutional and humanitarian implications. (2026-10-09) [single source]
  21. Super PAC supporting Darline Graham aired an anti-transgender attack ad against South Carolina Senate candidate Annie Andrews: A coordinated anti-trans attack ad in a competitive Senate race weaponizes culture-war rhetoric against vulnerable communities to polarize the electorate. (2026-10-09)
  22. Trump made inflammatory statements accusing Somali immigrants in Minnesota of crime and urging residents to "fight back": Presidential rhetoric targeting a specific immigrant community and urging vigilante action creates conditions for community harm and undermines equal protection. (2026-10-09)
  23. Federal agents arrested protesters attempting to prevent destruction of an ancient cottonwood tree during border wall construction: Arresting protesters engaged in civil disobedience against a federal infrastructure project raises questions about the scope of permitted dissent. (2026-10-09) [single source]
  24. Representative Austin Scott, Senator Thom Tillis, and Senator Jon Ossoff publicly criticized the Pentagon's plan to livestream a military execution as obscene and comparable to dictatorship tactics: Bipartisan congressional criticism of a planned public execution broadcast reflects shared concern over state-sanctioned spectacle and the dignity of capital punishment. (2026-10-09)

Information, Memory and Manipulation

  1. Trump White House repeatedly barred Politico and CNN from the Air Force One press pool despite a court order requiring reinstated access: Continued exclusion of news organizations after a judicial order violates First Amendment press-access rights and signals defiance of court authority. (2026-10-04)
  2. Popular Information launched PaidForBy.info, a tool letting voters identify who funds political mailers and ads: A public transparency tool closes an information gap in political advertising, enabling citizens to scrutinize campaign spending and funding sources. (2026-10-04) [single source]
  3. Changpeng Zhao publicly advocated for dictatorship over democracy as more efficient in a New York Times interview: A Trump-pardoned businessman with family financial ties publicly endorsing authoritarian governance signals ideological alignment undermining democratic norms. (2026-10-06)
  4. Trump accused the New York Times of doctoring a photograph of his Miami club and called for arrests of media outlets for dishonesty: False accusations against a major newspaper combined with threats of criminal prosecution attack press independence and normalize punishing unfavorable coverage. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  5. Trump posted carefully cropped rally photographs to dispute news coverage showing sparse attendance: Deliberate visual manipulation to contradict documented news photographs undermines factual accountability and public trust in official communications. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  6. Senator Mike Lee suggested without evidence that U.S. government funding, possibly through Fauci, was involved in a Russian plague researcher's death: An unfounded conspiracy theory from a sitting senator spreads disinformation and erodes public trust in scientific institutions. (2026-10-06) [single source]
  7. Trump publicly pressured Fox News over interviews with Democratic candidates, calling coverage "softball" and demanding more favorable treatment: Direct presidential pressure on a television network to alter editorial decisions represents an attempt to control news coverage of political opponents. (2026-10-06)
  8. Trump declared that use of the term "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" makes someone "THE ENEMY": Declaring standard terminology enemy speech reflects an attempt to enforce linguistic conformity across federal communications and punish deviation from official framing. (2026-10-08)
  9. Trump posted false claims that Senate candidate James Talarico was "missing in action" while Talarico was recovering from illness: Spreading false claims about an opponent's whereabouts and health represents deliberate disinformation intended to damage a political rival before an election. (2026-10-08)
  10. Texas PAC and V-PAC distributed campaign mailers with acknowledged false claims about Senate and gubernatorial candidates' policy positions: Super PACs knowingly circulating false claims in campaign mailers distort voter understanding of candidates' actual positions during the final weeks before elections. (2026-10-09) [single source]
  11. Heather Honey and DHS placed an election denier in a prominent role directing investigations into alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the midterms: Assigning an election denier to lead voting-fraud investigations raises concerns that enforcement is driven by ideology rather than evidence of actual violations. (2026-10-09)
  12. David Schoen (Trump's lawyer) issued a statement attacking the Nobel Committee's award to Navi Pillay as a "phony" decision motivated by anti-American bias: An official attack on an international institution's independent judgment seeks to discredit accountability findings regarding allied military conduct. (2026-10-09)
